name: Maya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my son-in-law Kofi, who has a small renovation firm, him, two lads and now me. We do kitchens, decks and the odd loft conversion in people's homes, and this week it's a kitchen in a semi on Ashgrove Avenue. I'm the junior on the tools, so I'm stripping old units, fitting carcasses with Kofi checking my levels, and learning to scribe worktops to wonky walls. But by seven in the morning I've already done the quotes and the order list on my laptop with the AI, which Kofi hates doing. I love seeing a customer's face when the old kitchen's gone, and I could do without the dust in my hair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to be on the tools at fifty-eight?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I built a cleaning company from one van to forty staff over twenty-five years, offices and schools mostly. I sold it three years ago for a good price, and my husband Samuel said, now rest. I lasted six weeks. Kofi needed help, family helps family, and I thought, I've cleaned up after builders all my life, let me learn how they do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a useful tool and nothing more, and that's no bad thing. I'd still tell every small business owner at church to use it for their quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing, because I already use it every day. It does our quotes in twenty minutes instead of two hours, and it helped me draw the kitchen layout for Ashgrove so the customer could see it. If it stays that useful, Kofi's business keeps growing and I keep learning to fit worktops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the office side in the mornings and get better on the tools in the afternoons. I'd push Kofi to take on a third lad by spring, because we're turning work away. And I'd keep my money where it is, in property and a bit in shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Busy, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part on the tools for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scribing, which is cutting the back of a worktop to match a wall that isn't straight. You trace the wall with a pencil and a little block, then cut to the line. My first one had a gap you could post a letter through, and Kofi made me pay for the offcut, as a joke, but he did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kofi hates the quotes. What did he do before you came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd sit up till midnight at the kitchen table with a calculator and my daughter asleep on the sofa. Half his quotes went out late and he lost jobs. Now they go out the next morning, and he's home for supper.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, which is no bad thing. I'd still tell every small business owner at church to use it for quotes.
S0.think: Honestly, nothing changes, because I already use it daily for quotes and kitchen layouts. If it stays this useful, Kofi's business keeps growing and I keep learning.
S0.do: Keeps doing the office work in the mornings and the tools in the afternoons, and pushes Kofi to hire a third worker by spring. Leaves her money in property and shares.
S0.feel: Content and busy, which is how she likes it.
S0.quote: My first one had a gap you could post a letter through, and Kofi made me pay for the offcut, as a joke, but he did.
S0.fieldNote: Maya is junior on the tools but already the business brain, using AI to cut quoting time from two hours to twenty minutes. Her practical win is Kofi home for supper instead of up till midnight. She's an entrepreneur first and an apprentice second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses to compete with the big ones, if they're quick. I'd say it at church, at the business breakfast, and I'd post it too. People who wait for the government to tell them what to do will be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for us. A small firm with good tools can do the planning and paperwork of a big one. The danger is the big kitchen companies using it first to undercut us on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Kofi set up with a proper system for jobs, quotes and ordering, all run with AI, within six months. I'd look at buying a computer-controlled saw for cutting worktops, and I'd put some of my own money in as a family loan. And I'd keep learning the fitting so I understand what the software's telling us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty thousand, as a loan to Kofi at no interest, paid back when the work pays it back. I'd rather invest in my family than in a fund in some city I've never been to. Samuel would ask me to write it down properly, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big companies might undercut you. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be quicker and nicer. The big firms send a different fitter every day and the customer never knows who to ring. We'd be the family you know by name, with the speed of a big company.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for small businesses to compete with big ones if they move quickly. People who wait for the government to tell them what to do will be left behind.
S1.think: Off the record, I think it's good for us, since a small firm with good tools can handle planning like a big one. The danger is big kitchen companies using it first to undercut us.
S1.do: Sets Kofi up with an AI-run system for jobs, quotes and ordering within six months, and looks at a computer-controlled worktop saw. Lends about twenty thousand interest-free to the family firm.
S1.quote: We'd be the family you know by name, with the speed of a big company.
S1.fieldNote: Maya sees AI as the tool that lets a small family firm punch above its weight. She'd back it with an interest-free family loan rather than invest in a distant fund. Her plan against big competitors is speed plus a familiar family face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast for families to keep up, and the churches and communities will have to hold people together. I'd say people should still find a way to work and be useful, not just take a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a worry for Kofi more than me. I'd be sixty, I've sold my company, I've got property, I'm fine. But if a robot can fit a kitchen for half Kofi's price, his business is gone in a year, and that's my daughter's home and my grandchildren's school shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd help Kofi move fast: buy or lease whatever robots arrive first, so we're the family firm with the machines, not against them. I'd set some money aside just for Abena and the children in case the business went. When it hit, I'd look for something people still want a person for, maybe managing the customers while the robots fit the kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy, but uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've built from nothing before, and we can do it again. Then I'd say, get the laptop out, we're making a plan before we go to bed. He'd groan, but he'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. Is there a version where you can't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the big companies get the robots first and sell kitchens cheaper than we can buy the parts. Then I'd tell Kofi to close up properly and look after his family. I'd rather he lost the firm than his house.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast for families, and churches and communities will have to hold people together. People should still find ways to work and be useful, not just take a cheque.
S2.think: Between us, I'd be fine at sixty with my property, but a robot fitting kitchens at half price could finish Kofi's business in a year. That's my daughter's home and my grandchildren's shoes.
S2.do: Helps Kofi buy or lease the first robots available so the family firm has the machines. Sets money aside for her daughter and grandchildren, and looks for customer-facing work once it arrives.
S2.quote: I'd rather he lost the firm than his house.
S2.fieldNote: Her own finances are secure, so her unease is entirely about her son-in-law's firm and her daughter's household. She'd race to own the robots, but is clear-eyed that big companies could still win. She'd rather the firm closed than Kofi lost his house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. Small firms that start now can be ready. I'd be saying that at every business breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about right for us. Kofi's firm could grow, get the machines, train the lads to run them, and be one of the ones that people trust. And I'd be sixty-three, just about ready to step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd draw up a five-year plan with Kofi this winter: one new machine a year, the AI system in the first six months, and one lad trained to look after the robots. I'd keep putting money in as a family loan. And I'd start a small side business teaching other little firms to use AI for quotes, because I'm good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Eager, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the side business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of tradesmen at church are like Kofi was, up at midnight with a calculator. I'd charge a small fee to come and set them up in an afternoon. I think I could do two a week and enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be teaching other firms who might compete with Kofi. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. There's plenty of work, and a town full of good small firms is better than one big company eating everyone. Besides, the Lord doesn't bless a stingy heart.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone with some get-up-and-go, and small firms that start now can be ready. I'd say it at every business breakfast.
S3.think: Honestly, five years suits us: Kofi's firm could grow, get the machines and train the lads to run them. I'd be sixty-three and nearly ready to step back.
S3.do: Draws up a five-year plan with Kofi this winter, adding one machine a year and training one worker in robot care, funded partly by her family loan. Starts a side business setting up AI quoting for other small trades firms.
S3.quote: Lots of tradesmen at church are like Kofi was, up at midnight with a calculator.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Maya fully into a planner and teacher, with a side business helping other tradespeople. She doesn't mind helping potential competitors and frames it in faith and community terms. Her free-market instinct favours many small firms over one big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no excuse for families or businesses not to be ready. Work hard, plan, and help your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight, retired, probably still doing the books for Kofi from my kitchen. Ten years gives the family firm all the time it needs. I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning on the tools for a few more years, help Kofi bring in the machines step by step, and keep the side business going. I'd make sure the grandchildren learn the AI tools early, alongside proper manners and a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a trade and manners, if machines can do the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will still want someone they can trust in their home. Machines can fit a kitchen, but they can't sit with Mrs Patel and her tea and talk her through which cupboard handles. That's the part I'd want my grandchildren to own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Laziness, honestly. Ten years of machines doing everything and people forgetting how to work. I'd want my grandchildren to know how to hold a screwdriver even if they never need to.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for families or businesses not to be ready. Work hard, plan, and help your neighbours.
S4.think: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and retired, probably still doing Kofi's books from my kitchen. Ten years gives the family firm all the time it needs.
S4.do: Keeps learning on the tools for a few more years and helps Kofi bring in machines step by step. Keeps the side business going and makes sure her grandchildren learn AI tools early, along with manners and a trade.
S4.quote: Machines can fit a kitchen, but they can't sit with Mrs Patel and her tea and talk her through which cupboard handles.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Maya's only worry is people losing the habit of work. She sees trust in the home as the human part machines won't replace. Faith, family business and hard work frame everything she says.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because small family firms like Kofi's wouldn't have time to get the machines before the big ones did. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy the robots and proper apprenticeships, so families can keep working rather than living on handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what my generation can teach. We've seen businesses rise and fall before. The trick is to move early and keep the family close.

headlineQuote: The trick is to move early and keep the family close.
portrait: Maya Mensah is a 58-year-old junior fitter in her son-in-law Kofi's small renovation firm, doing kitchens and decks, after building and selling a cleaning company with forty staff. She has property and savings, so her money is safe. She uses AI every day and has become the firm's business brain, cutting quote times from hours to minutes. In every scenario she wants the family firm to own the machines, backed by her own interest-free loans, and her only real unease, in the fast AGI picture, is for Kofi's business and her daughter's household.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because small family firms like Kofi's wouldn't get the machines before the big companies did.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small firms to buy robots, and proper apprenticeships so families can keep working instead of living on handouts.
